KEY MESSAGE 1...Overall pattern is quickly getting complex this
afternoon. Latest analysis today shows a potent sub- tropical 
jet ongoing with a maxima centered over the northern Gulf of
America and Florida Peninsula. Deep upper trough is digging into
the southern plains and taking on an increasingly neutral tilt,
while a separate low and attendant jet streak dives out of the
Canadian prairies and tracks towards the Ohio River Valley. 
The latter two features are forecast to undergo a complex 
interaction over the eastern CONUS through Thanksgiving, with 
the Plains trough digging further into the Gulf Coast and taking
on a negative tilt as it interacts with the OH Valley low. We 
will see a similar evolution at the mid- levels with two potent 
shortwave troughs.

This overall pattern favors surface cyclogenesis along the 
Southeastern coast starting tomorrow morning. Trends continue to
favor a slightly more inland track than offshore although the
low itself will not be especially deep - around or slightly
below 1000 mb.

The low will track northward and deepen as it moves towards the
Carolinas. Despite its expected central pressure, it will to 
buttress a very strong surface high (around 1040 mb) wedged 
over the mid- Atlantic. The resulting pressure gradient will 
bring very strong ENE winds to the region, peaking tomorrow 
night into the early morning hours on Thu, and most acutely felt
over the Outer Banks with gusts up to 50 mph tomorrow night. 
Gusts up to 35 mph are also possible inland. This threat
necessitated the issuance of a Wind Advisory for all coastal
counties starting tomorrow afternoon. The higher winds also 
heightens concerns for coastal flooding...see KEY MESSAGE 3 for 
more details on this.

The cyclone will also pull up a plume of very deep moisture 
from the Atlantic with PWATs forecast to exceed 2" (per 
climatology this is roughly 300%+ of normal for late November). 
With the strong ascent aloft, heavy rainfall is likely. Both
deterministic and probabilistic guidance continue to shift in a
more aggressive direction for rainfall, particularly for the
Crystal Coast and Outer Banks. REFS probabilities of seeing more
than 5" of rain in 24 hours are an eye-popping 80%+ for this 
area; the NBM is slightly less aggressive but still shows a
notable 30-40% for the same threshold. Inland locales are not as
likely to see such amounts but are still likely (70-80% chance)
to see amounts exceeding 2". 

It should be noted this area of higher rainfall will depend on 
a combination of the low track as well as any embedded 
convective elements. Additionally, a potential failure mode may
be convective that develops over the Gulf Stream early in the
event and effectively robs mainland NC of deeper moisture,
reducing overall rainfall amounts. Given such strong synoptic
forcing in place this risk appears unlikely but will have to be
monitored. Still, this level of rainfall will pose a threat of
flash flooding, especially for urban corridors, despite ongoing
severe to extreme drought. A Flood Watch has been issued for all
areas except the inner coastal plain starting tomorrow
afternoon.

Risk of thunder overall remains low with only marginal
instability available - less than 500 J/kg. Still, areas closer
to the coast, esp the OBX, will have to be monitored for a 
localized svr threat, as strong cells over the Gulf Stream 
could approach the islands providing an iso tornado or 
waterspout threat overnight Wed. 

Low pres arrives Thur, and with it, a sharp reduction in winds
as they veer to the south and weaken to less than 20 mph as the
area becomes dry slotted.

KEY MESSAGE 2...ENC is currently experiencing the next round of
king tides this week with an increase in antecedant water 
levels. These are expected to peak through Thursday and then 
begin tapering off Friday and esp the weekend, and will be 
slightly higher than the cycle that occurred in October. Water
levels will remain elevated tonight as strong winds are ongoing
behind yesterday's strong cold front.

Tomorrow night is much more concerning as the approaching low 
pres brings and even further inc in NE to E winds to gales 
across the sounds and inland rivers (Pamlico and Neuse), and 
brings the threat for impactful coastal flooding for these 
areas. Most tidal locations across ENC are likely to see at 
least minor to moderate impacts, with the risk for major impacts
for more typically vulnerable locations given forecast 
strengthening NE to E winds up the rivers. Interests should 
continue to closely monitor forecasts through the coming days. 
With the decrease in winds on Thursday expected, the flood 
threat for the inland rivers and southern Pamlico Sound may 
begin to ease, but oceanside impacts will cont on the OBX into 
late week.
